summary: Updates the IP Performance Metrics framework from RFC 2330 for IPv6 and IPv4-IPv6 coexistence. It extends standard-formed packets to include IPv6, deprecates the minimal IP packet definition, and augments the aspects that distinguish measurement types.

eli5.summary: The rules for measuring internet speed were written for the old address style. This updates them to work with the new style too.

questions: how does nat affect network measurements
subtitle: Brings IPv6 and IPv4-IPv6 translation into the IP Performance Metrics framework's idea of a standard-formed test packet.

tldr.problem: The IPPM framework in RFC 2330 defined a standard-formed packet only for IPv4, even though its authors planned to add version 6, and translation, NAT and extension headers can change test packets on the way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8468 adds IPv6 criteria to the definition of a standard-formed packet, widens the Type-P notion for packet features, deprecates the minimal IP packet, and requires that any changes to Type-P along the path be reported.
tldr.outcome: Measurement designers get clear IPv6 rules and a list of coexistence pitfalls, while ROHC and 6LoWPAN packets are left out of scope.

today: RFC 8468 is an Informational document that updates RFC 2330, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its definition of a standard-formed packet refers to RFC 8200 for IPv6.

sections.title: Why Update the IPPM Framework
sections.content:
The IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) working group created its metric framework in RFC 2330, and the RFC says it has stood the test of time. Section 15 of RFC 2330 defines a standard-formed packet, but never extended it to IPv6, even though its authors wrote that the version field is 4 and "later, we will expand this to include 6". IPv6 Extension Headers and header compression are growing in use, so this memo supplies the update.

The scope is to expand the Type-P examples in Section 13 and the standard-formed definition in Section 15 of RFC 2330. Passive and hybrid active/passive measurement are deferred to future work.
sections.eli5: The old measuring rulebook promised to explain the new address style later. This document finally does that.

sections.title: Packets of Type-P
sections.content:
Many metrics give different results depending on the packets used: well-known TCP ports versus unreserved UDP ports, bad checksums, or a particular TTL or Hop Limit. Packets can be treated specially by nodes using Diffserv, ECN, Router Alert, Hop-by-Hop extensions, Flow Labels, firewalls or RSVP. So a metric name carries Type-P, such as IP-Type-P-connectivity, to remind the reader which kind of packet was measured.

If the Type-P information seen at the destination differs from the source, the modified values MUST be noted and reported. Packet length may change if headers are converted or Extension Headers are added or removed. For Neighbor Discovery tests the Hop Limit of 255 matters, so it MUST be part of the Type-P.

Load balancing is a special difficulty. Routers hash header fields to pick one of several parallel paths, and a black-box measurement does not know which fields are used. Knowing the load balancer's flow definition is a prerequisite for repeatable measurements.
sections.eli5: If you race different kinds of toy cars, the result depends on the car. So every result should say which car was used and note if the car was changed along the track.

sections.title: Standard-Formed IPv4 and IPv6 Packets
sections.content:
A packet is standard-formed only if it meets all REQUIRED criteria. For both versions: a valid IP header, not a fragment, source and destination matching the intended ones (multicast allowed), and a valid checksum and fields in any transport header.

For IPv4 the version field is 4, the IHL is at least 5 with a correct checksum, the total length matches header plus payload, TTL is sufficient or at the maximum of 255, and there are no IP options unless noted. For IPv6 the version field is 6, the total length is the 40-octet header plus payload length, the payload length (including Extension Headers) conforms to the specifications, Hop Limit is sufficient or the maximum of 255, Extension Headers are correct and in standard order, and all parameters are in the IANA IPv6 Parameters registry.

A packet described as "length of B octets" must satisfy 0 <= B <= 65535. Jumbograms with the Jumbogram Payload option MUST be considered standard-formed. Changing Diffserv, ECN or Flow Label does not affect standard-formed status. Path MTU Discovery or Packetization Layer PMTUD is recommended to prevent fragmentation.

6LoWPAN and ROHC are considered out of scope of the evaluation because their fragmentation, stateful compression and Type-P changes need substantial work. The RFC also deprecates the "minimal IP packet from A to B" of RFC 2330, since it has not been used in practice.
sections.eli5: A "proper" test packet must be built correctly, like a letter with a real address, the right stamp and a sensible size. Weird shortcuts are left for another day.

sections.title: Extension Headers, NAT and Translation
sections.content:
When IPv6 Extension Headers are present, intermediate nodes may inspect them, possibly dropping the packet or routing it by a suboptimal path, which can make measurements unreliable. Hop-by-Hop options may be changed in transit. Insertion or deletion of headers is not endorsed by current standards but may happen, so tools should be prepared and notify users. A change in packet length or header modification REQUIRES a new Type-P to be reported with the results. RFC 8250 endorses the IPv6 Destination Option for measurement purposes.

Translation, NAT, encapsulation or header compression along the path may change Type-P, and all these changes MUST be reported. The RFC lists consequences: modified headers, an unpredictable NAT effect on latency, variable delay because intermediate nodes create internal state (the first packet of a stream may be slower, and idle gaps can erase state), and delay differences caused by changed packet length. Some of these effects can be the purpose of a test.
sections.eli5: Things in the middle of the road can swap your car for a different one, or slow the first car down. If that happens, the measurement report must say so.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The security considerations for any active measurement of live paths apply here, with RFC 4656 and RFC 5357 cited. The RFC argues that the sensitive information available to observers is greatly reduced with active techniques in scope, while passive observation of user traffic raises many privacy issues, and points to the LMAP framework in RFC 7594. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Measuring with your own test packets reveals much less about people than watching their real traffic does.
